steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on LPFormer, a LiDAR-only 3D human pose estimation transformer built on a multi-task network. Explain why LiDAR-based pose estimation is hard and what previous methods rely on, the gap with image-based top-down methods, our two-stage design, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. LiDAR-based human pose estimation and the problem with 2D weak supervision
2. Top-down HPE in images and the backbone gap for LiDAR (BEV features)
3. LPFormer: two-stage framework, LiDAR only, 3D annotations only
4. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. LiDAR HPE
- HPE popular in image/video domain, wide applications
- 3D data (LiDAR point cloud) less attention: accurate 3D annotations hard to acquire
- previous LiDAR HPE methods: weakly-supervised, use 2D annotations
- assume precise camera-LiDAR calibration
- small annotation/calibration errors -> large errors in 3D -> affect training
- perspective view variation: lifting 2D annotations to 3D loses visibility info

2. Top-down and the backbone gap
- image HPE dominated by top-down: detect human box, then single-person pose from cropped features
- gap in backbone between 2D and 3D detectors
- LiDAR detectors use projected bird's-eye view (BEV) features -> lower compute
- but lose separable features in height dimension, crucial for HPE
- effective use of learned object features for HPE unexplored

3. LPFormer
- complete two-stage top-down 3D HPE; only LiDAR point cloud input; trained only on 3D annotations
- stage 1: previous state-of-the-art LiDAR multitask network; human boxes + fine-grained voxel features at smaller scale
- stage 2: point-level, voxel-level, object-level features inside each box; light-weighted keypoint transformer regresses keypoints
- HPE integrates into LiDAR multi-task learning framework (Figure 1); state-of-the-art without image features/annotations

4. Contributions
- first end-to-end 3D HPE network with only LiDAR input and 3D annotations
- keypoint transformer in unified LiDAR perception network; extends multitask framework to HPE with minimal overhead
- state-of-the-art on large-scale datasets; first place on Waymo Open Dataset Pose Estimation leaderboard; beats camera-based and multi-modal methods on validation set

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Human pose estimation (HPE) has become very popular in the image and video domain because it has a wide range of applications. But pose estimation with 3D data, like LiDAR point clouds, has gotten less attention, because it is difficult to get accurate 3D annotations. Because of this, previous methods on LiDAR-based HPE usually rely on weakly-supervised approaches that use 2D annotations. These approaches often assume that the camera and the LiDAR sensor are precisely calibrated. But in real-world scenarios, small errors in the annotations or the calibration can turn into big errors in 3D space, and that affects the training of the network. Also, because the perspective view varies, it is hard to accurately recover important visibility information just by lifting 2D annotations into 3D space.

In image-based HPE, the main approach is the top-down method, where you first detect the human bounding box and then predict the single-person pose from the cropped features. However, there is a big gap in the backbone network between the 2D detector and the 3D detector. Most LiDAR object detectors use projected bird's-eye view (BEV) features to detect objects, which reduces computational costs. But this loses the separable features in the height dimension, and those are crucial for human pose estimation. How to use the learned object features effectively for HPE is still unexplored.

3. LPFormer
- two-stage top-down 3D HPE; LiDAR point cloud only; 3D annotations only
- stage 1: previous state-of-the-art LiDAR multitask network -> human boxes + fine-grained voxel features
- stage 2: point/voxel/object-level features in each box -> light-weighted keypoint transformer regresses keypoints
- HPE fits into LiDAR multi-task framework (Figure 1); state-of-the-art, no image features or annotations

4. Contributions
- first end-to-end 3D HPE network, LiDAR input + 3D annotations only
- keypoint transformer in unified LiDAR perception network, minimal overhead
- state-of-the-art; first on Waymo Open Dataset Pose Estimation leaderboard; beats camera-based and multi-modal methods on validation set

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Human pose estimation (HPE) has become very popular in the image and video domain because it has a wide range of applications. But pose estimation with 3D data, like LiDAR point clouds, has gotten less attention, because it is difficult to get accurate 3D annotations. Because of this, previous methods on LiDAR-based HPE usually rely on weakly-supervised approaches that use 2D annotations. These approaches often assume that the camera and the LiDAR sensor are precisely calibrated. But in real-world scenarios, small errors in the annotations or the calibration can turn into big errors in 3D space, and that affects the training of the network. Also, because the perspective view varies, it is hard to accurately recover important visibility information just by lifting 2D annotations into 3D space.

In image-based HPE, the main approach is the top-down method, where you first detect the human bounding box and then predict the single-person pose from the cropped features. However, there is a big gap in the backbone network between the 2D detector and the 3D detector. Most LiDAR object detectors use projected bird's-eye view (BEV) features to detect objects, which reduces computational costs. But this loses the separable features in the height dimension, and those are crucial for human pose estimation. How to use the learned object features effectively for HPE is still unexplored.

In this paper we present LPFormer, a complete two-stage top-down 3D human pose estimation framework that only uses LiDAR point cloud as input and is trained only on 3D annotations. In the first stage, we use the design of the previous state-of-the-art LiDAR multitask network, which can predict human object bounding boxes accurately while also generating fine-grained voxel features at a smaller scale. The second stage extracts point-level, voxel-level, and object-level features from the point cloud inside each predicted bounding box, and regresses the keypoints with a light-weighted keypoint transformer network. Our approach shows that complex HPE tasks can be integrated seamlessly into the LiDAR multi-task learning framework (as shown in Figure 1), and it gets state-of-the-art performance without needing image features or annotations. The main contributions of this paper are:

- We present the first end-to-end 3D HPE network that depends only on LiDAR input and 3D annotations.

- Our keypoint transformer can be integrated into a unified LiDAR perception network, which extends a strong multitask framework proposed before to HPE tasks with only minimal computational overhead.

- Our experiments on large-scale datasets show state-of-the-art performance. LPFormer is currently in first place on the Waymo Open Dataset Pose Estimation leaderboard. Our approach also beats all previous camera-based and multi-modal methods on the validation set.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Human pose estimation (HPE) has gained significant popularity in the image and video domain due to its wide range of applications. However, pose estimation using 3D data, such as LiDAR point clouds, has received less attention because of the difficulty of acquiring accurate 3D annotations. As a result, previous methods [1,2,3] on LiDAR-based HPE commonly rely on weakly-supervised approaches that utilize 2D annotations. These approaches often assume precise calibration between the camera and the LiDAR sensor. In real-world scenarios, however, small errors in annotation or calibration can propagate into significant errors in 3D space and affect the training of the network. In addition, due to variations in the perspective view, it is difficult to accurately recover important visibility information by simply lifting 2D annotations into 3D space.

In image-based HPE, the dominant approach is the top-down method [4], which first detects the human bounding box and then predicts the single-person pose from the cropped features. However, there is a significant gap in the backbone network between 2D and 3D detectors. Most LiDAR object detectors use projected bird's-eye view (BEV) features to detect objects, which helps reduce computational costs. This leads to the loss of separable features in the height dimension that are crucial for human pose estimation. How to make effective use of learned object features for HPE remains unexplored.

In this paper, we present LPFormer, a complete two-stage top-down 3D human pose estimation framework that uses only LiDAR point clouds as input and is trained solely on 3D annotations. In the first stage, we adopt the design of the previous state-of-the-art LiDAR multitask network [5,6], which can accurately predict human object bounding boxes while generating fine-grained voxel features at a smaller scale. The second stage extracts point-level, voxel-level, and object-level features from the point cloud inside each predicted bounding box and regresses the keypoints with a light-weighted keypoint transformer network. Our approach demonstrates that complex HPE tasks can be seamlessly integrated into the LiDAR multi-task learning framework (as shown in Figure 1), achieving state-of-the-art performance without image features or annotations. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

- We present the first end-to-end 3D HPE network that depends only on LiDAR input and 3D annotations.

- Our proposed keypoint transformer can be integrated into a unified LiDAR perception network, extending a previously proposed strong multitask framework to HPE tasks with only minimal computational overhead.

- Our experimental results on large-scale datasets show state-of-the-art performance. Notably, LPFormer currently ranks first on the Waymo Open Dataset Pose Estimation leaderboard, and our approach outperforms all previous camera-based and multi-modal methods on the validation set.

References:
[1] J. Zheng, X. Shi, A. Gorban, J. Mao, Y. Song, C. R. Qi, T. Liu, V. Chari, A. Cornman, Y. Zhou, et al. , “Multi-modal 3d human pose estimation with 2d weak supervision in autonomous driving,” in CVPRW , 2022.
[2] P. Cong, Y. Xu, Y. Ren, J. Zhang, L. Xu, J. Wang, J. Yu, and Y. Ma, “Weakly supervised 3d multi-person pose estimation for large-scale scenes based on monocular camera and single lidar,” in AAAI , 2023.
[3] A. Zanfir, M. Zanfir, A. Gorban, J. Ji, Y. Zhou, D. Anguelov, and C. Sminchisescu, “Hum3dil: Semi-supervised multi-modal 3d humanpose estimation for autonomous driving,” in CoRL , 2022.
[4] K. Sun, B. Xiao, D. Liu, and J. Wang, “Deep high-resolution representation learning for human pose estimation,” in CVPR , 2019.
[5] D. Ye, Z. Zhou, W. Chen, Y. Xie, Y. Wang, P. Wang, and H. Foroosh, “Lidarmultinet: Towards a unified multi-task network for lidar perception,” in AAAI , 2023.
[6] Z. Zhou, D. Ye, W. Chen, Y. Xie, Y. Wang, P. Wang, and H. Foroosh, “Lidarformer: A unified transformer-based multi-task network for lidar perception,” in ICRA , 2024.
